utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances for today, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Tom Hannis, along with Alex Demirdjian and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic, appearing for Stanisic Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. If there is nothing that need delay us, may we -- should the usher escort the witness in?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Our first witness is Mico Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. I trust you can hear me in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The solemn declaration that you have just made, exposes you to the pain of the penalties for perjury should you give false or misleading testimony to this Tribunal which is a lawfully constituted criminal Tribunal under international law. I would, first of all, ask you to state for the record your name, your date of birth, and your ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milorad Davidovic is my name. I was born on 13th of February, 1951 in Opre, Bosnia-Herzegovina. I permanently reside in Belgrade, in Vospovra Jevremova [phoen] Street, number 31.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a degree there political science and another degree in speech therapy. I worked as a policeman and I spent my entire career working for the police. I'm a retiree now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you testified previously before this Tribunal or before any of the courts in countries that comprise the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I was already before this Tribunal in the proceedings against Mr. Krajisnik. Also, I was a witness in the court in Belgrade, the special court for war crimes, that is, in the case against the Yellow Wasps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you sir. In which case I need only remind you of our procedure which is that the side calling you will begin by asking you questions - in this case it is the Prosecution. After which the side opposite, the Defence respectively of Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Zupljanin would have a right to ask you questions. The Prosecution could have questions you in re-examination and at any point the Benches may have questions of you. The pattern of sitting that we follow and your testimony is scheduled for mornings this week so it means that at the end of the day, the sitting day would be at 1.45. But there are two scheduled breaks in between that, both for the comfort of the witness and counsel and everybody else involved but also for technical reasons having to do with changing the tapes which can only run for 90 minutes before they have to be changed. So the -- at approximately 90-minute intervals, actually, it's a little shorter than that there would be a 20-minute break and we would resume until we rise for the day, as I said at 1.45. Notwithstanding those scheduled break that I have indicated, if for any reason you need to request a break before the scheduled time, if you indicate that to us, we will certainly accommodate you. And with that, I would ask Mr. Hannis to begin his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to begin by addressing some of your prior evidence that is being offered in this trial pursuant to Rule 92 ter. You told the Judge that you previously testified in the case against Mr. Krajisnik. Before coming to court today, did you have a chance to review your testimony that you gave in that case by listening to it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I read it, and I listened to it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after having done that, are you able to tell us that you were satisfied that it was -- it was an accurate account of your evidence, and would you give the same answers today if you were asked the same questions?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will be moving to tender that evidence at the end of his testimony, and those transcripts for the dates he testified in Krajisnik are 65 ter numbers 10474 through 10478.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Davidovic, in addition, the Prosecution is proposing to offer evidence that you gave in a written statement and some additional information. That written statement reflects interviews that were conducted with you in November 2004 and January 2005. And I think you have a hard copy of that document in front of you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And before coming to court today, did you have a chance to review it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I've already read it over the course of the past few days. So, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during proofing, I just wanted to go through with you, there were a few -- there were a few items where in our conversations you made some -- some minor correction. If you could look at paragraph 39, first of all. And paragraph 39 talks about --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm sorry, Mr. Hannis, is the document in the courtroom. I mean, for the benefit of the accused, if you can call it up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It is. And this is 65 ter number 10472.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Paragraph 39 is where you talk delivering some equipment from Belgrade to Pale. And you previously said February or March of 1992. And during proofing, you indicated that it may have been April, as you remember the trees were green at that time of year; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have to clarify that, if I may just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before making this written statement I had said to you that I cannot remember exactly which time-period it was. Will it be a month sooner or later, I'm simply not in a position to say because it's been a long time. I was very busy, I did lots of work, so I can't remember the exact dates and the names of people. It is hard for me to remember that now with a high degree of precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm truly sorry. Can we have the paragraph 39 which Mr. Hannis is referring to, and the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What is it you're requesting?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The -- on the monitor we have paragraphs from 32 to 34. Now it's changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh. It's page 11 in both of English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Davidovic. Yes I recall you do -- do telling us that. I think you also testified about that in Krajisnik. At the time of these events in 1992, is it correct that you -- you made a number of notes and reports contemporaneously with those events?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, I had to report to my superiors and those who had sent me out on certain missions. So I wrote up notes on all the tasks I carried out. There were several of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And -- and had you a personal collection of -- of your notes and copies of those reports in -- in your personal possession for a number of years after those events?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Quite a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you no longer have them.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I no longer have them. When my apartment was searched by the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, that documentation was found. Everything was seized. And I have submitted to you a copy, certifying that all of this material had been seized. There was quite a bit of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it's never been returned to you since that time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Your Honours that's reflected in his written statement and I won't go into any more detail about it at that time. One other change. At paragraph 43, this is about assistance to the new RS MUP in April 1992. It's at page 12 of both the B/C/S and English. And you talked about a meeting with Mr. Kertes and Mr. Gracanin. You say it was about the 6th of April. However, at -- the proofing note indicates that after you had a reviewed a couple of intercepted telephone conversations it became clear to you that that meeting must have been later because those telephone conversations in May, early May, 1992, are in your memory, ones that took place just a few days after your meeting with Gracanin and Kertes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I clarified all of that for you, in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Having noted those corrections, can you tell us that you're satisfied that your written statement is an accurate account to your -- to the best of your knowledge and memory of the events and they're described in that written statement; and would you give the same answers, if asked the same questions?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that's 65 ter 10472 and 10473 which we'll move to tender at the end of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, with those clarifications, I would like to move on and just ask you about some specific events that perhaps you can elaborate or clarify or expand on a little bit. We have in your -- your prior testimony and your statement some of your background. You began working in the police in 1974. In 1982, you went to Sarajevo to help with the security for the 1984 Olympics; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: By my math, you were aged 31 at the time. That's -- that seem's pretty young for such a big job.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we were recruited young and we started working at a very young age, so they gave us this opportunity to prove ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And in 1988, you say you were nominated for a management position with the federal SUP but you didn't take up that job until 1991. I'd like to show you a document. It's Exhibit P516. This will be up on your screen in a moment, Mr. Davidovic. Prior to going to work for the federal SUP, what was your job at that time in the police?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, let me answer the question from the monitor. What was written here by Momo Mandic, that he gave his consent, I have to explain that. It wasn't that Momo Mandic gave me his consent to go to the federal SUP. Two years before this document was written, I had the consent or, rather, the decision of the republican MUP collegium to be sent to the federal MUP. However, I delayed that because of certain things that happened in the SUP. There was some changes of personnel. These important changes took place, and so on, and then when I was replaced, then I offered my services to Petar Gracanin and he said that that decision was valid and that I could come there and that is how I transferred to the federal SUP and started working there. And then I was sent from the federal SUP from the personnel department to Sarajevo to get all my personal documents and that is when Momo Mandic wrote up this accompanying document, although he is not the one who made the decision. It was Muhamed, the former minister of the interior who did. So I would like to do away with any possible suspicion that it was Momo Mandic who sent me. Actually when I went, they complained because I and Sredoje Novic, who was under-secretary for state security Yugoslavia at the time, were being sent there. Then Minister Delimustafic, Avdo Hebib, and I don't know who else, complained from Bosnia-Herzegovina and therefore he was no longer under-secretary for state security in the former Yugoslavia although that had been made public in the "Official Gazette" but still the appointment did not come through. However they accepted that my appointment go through and that I remain there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, when the witness is speaking could all other microphones be switched off. We with barely understand what the witness is saying. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before you left to go work for the federal --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Hannis. I note the interpreter's note. And I was having actually problems following what the witness was saying. If you can please instruct the witness to -- to speak slowly and -- and clearly into the microphone so we can have actually what he said. Because a part of his testimony has not been recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, the interpreters indicated that it would be helpful if you could speak more slowly and it looks like one of your microphones is off. I'm not sure if that's part of the problem.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Exactly. It's on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So try to speak a bit more slowly if you can. After --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Zecevic, you indicate that a portion of the witness's testimony was not recorded. Is it sufficiently significant that Mr. Hannis should perhaps be asked to have the witness repeat his answer in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, either that or we can address it in cross-examination. Whatever is Mr. Hannis's preference.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll leave it to the Defence to follow up, if there is something additional that they want in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Immediately before you went to take up work with the federal SUP, what had been your job in the police?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was commander of the police station Ugljevik, then the chief of the crime prevention service in the security service in Tuzla. Then I was commander of the traffic police station in Bijeljina. Then I was appointed commander of the general police station in Bijeljina. Then I was appointed co-ordinator of both stations, and during the last six months I was chief of the public security in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could you explain for us briefly what the federal SUP was and what its relationship was with the republican MUPs in the various republics of the former Yugoslavia. And I see your other microphone has gone off again. Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear that conversation but -- okay, I see it's off again and I guess that's the way we want it to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We're advised that the technicians have switched off one of the microphone because the witness's proximity to the microphone means there is a distortion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Davidovic, we will work with one microphone with you then. Do you need to hear my question again or can you answer?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: You need not repeat. I'll explain briefly. The federal SUP was federal agency of the former Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. One of its purposes was to provide security to federal institutions and to embassies and consular offices abroad to provide security to public officials and to perform other work in institutions of special importance to former Yugoslavia, that was part of the public security and within the area of state security, it was the main centre that co-ordinated and guided the work of these services. That is to put it very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And we see from your written statement that once you got to the federal SUP and began working there, one of the tasks that you took up was work on a commission, a federal commission, that was established to visit Security Services Centres and SJBs in Bosnia. And what was the purpose of that commission?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was more than one such commission. The first one was established with a view to preventing war conflicts that's arose in Croatia. After that commission returned from Croatia, another one was formed to go to Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to establish, together with the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, whether or not there were any violations of the Law on Internal Affairs regarding the security of citizens whether there were any [indiscernible] conflicts and whether the police was involved in them or preventing them, whether there was any increase or decrease in the reserve force of the police, and if so, in which authorities and which agencies and to co-ordinate the work between the police and the army with a view to establishing joint check-points, to check on the passage of motor vehicles, military or otherwise, and to defuse the tensions between the members of the army and the members of the police, primarily those of Muslim ethnicity, and commission carried out that work in all centres, some of them were stationed in -- in -- one range of centres and the others in -- in others.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your -- in your statement at paragraph 30, you're talking about an example of some of the changes in reserve police numbers seen in the Tuzla region. The question I have, near the end of that paragraph, you make references to the new SDS Bijeljina chief refused to surrender certain weapons. Who was that chief of the Bijeljina SUP at that time? Can you give us the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That was Predrag Jesuric, appointed by the SDS, the Serbian Democratic Party, and by a decision by Minister Delimustafic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that's the man who replaced you as police chief in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was he a professional policeman before receiving that appointment?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. He was never involved with the police. For a while he worked as a judge later as lawyer, although he had never been a lawyer until then. He was mostly involved in smuggling and worked as a foreign currency dealer. He had his own network of dealers, and, that's what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. At paragraph 34 you refer to the federal SUP Special Brigade. Can you tell us briefly what that brigade was?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Within the brigade which had 1100 -- sorry, 1.000 or 1200 men depending on the moment, they provided security for all federal institutions and institutions of special importance to Yugoslavia, all representative offices such embassies abroad, et cetera, security at workplaces for public officials at home and at work, et cetera. Within the brigade, there was also a battalion for special operations and that was a units for special purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what did the term "special purposes" cover? What kind of activities were those?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, a special unit had been established long before. It was only the only special unit in Yugoslavia. They were trained to react to terrorist incursions into the territory of Yugoslavia in open or closed spaces to prevent kidnaps and hijackings by terrorists again. They were trained for special tasks involving persons who would try to endanger the safety of other citizens and that's what they were trained for. That unit had around 100 mean. It had state-of-the-art equipment. The latest equipment and the people who worked there were 25 to 30 years old, extremely fit and extremely well trained.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did the federal brigade consist of men from all the various republics of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It included a regular segment that was replenished from the centre in Kamenica. Some men were provided by republics which contributed a number of men. The number varied from republic to republic but they all provided a certain complement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, after the -- the conflict in Bosnia started in early April, did you have occasion to be directed to have some participation in Bosnia by your bosses?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was not suggested to me. I had been to the newly established MUP of Republika Srpska on visits to offer assistance, in terms of materiel and equipment, and later I was officially sent by the official authorities there, and I had a clear assignment. And I did two tours there with part of the unit from the federal SUP in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is, the territory of Republika Srpska more specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before -- before going to the RS with -- with other members from your -- from your federal SUP brigade, had -- I think you have just told me you had made trips to the -- to the new RS MUP and helped with delivery of certain equipment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What kind of equipment did -- did you take?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Uniforms, helmets, shields, flak jackets, certain weapons and ammunition. Everything that the police needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Any communication equipment?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think there was some, but I don't know exactly. I know about the part that was taken from the brigade, such as uniforms and some additional equipment, such as armour helmet, et cetera. I suppose there were also communication systems but I think it was hand-held radios. I can't remember anything else, although I'm pretty sure there was more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 43 of your statement, you talk about meeting you had with Kertes and Gracanin. And you say at this meeting this was where you were instructed to -- to go to -- to the RS. First of all, can you tell the Court who Mr. Kertes was and what position he held at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the statement that I have before me, I don't see the paragraph 43. It must have been omitted in the typing but I can answer the question regardless of whether I see it before me or not. Mr. Kertes used to be member of the Presidency of the Republic of Serbia, and after finishing his term of office there, he was appointed to the federal SUP as assistant of the federal minister then federal [as interpreted] Gracanin, and he was in charge of public security and he was in charge of co-ordinating the work of security services within the federal SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, at page 12 I think, paragraph 43 is on page 12, both the -- of the English and the B/C/S. I think it's the bottom of your page 12, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't have page 12. It's missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Or maybe it is somewhere else in the batch of pages --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, you may be able to see it --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Not in its right place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You may be able to see it on the screen if you don't have a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is exactly why I'm up, because we don't have it on the screen. Maybe if you can --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's -- it's 65 ter 10472. I don't know if the usher can have a look to see if he can help to locate it. I ... Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Mr. Gracanin, what was his position?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gracanin was the federal minister of the interior. The most responsible person, the most highly placed person in the federal SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were you told why it was necessary for you to volunteer for this assignment?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Kertes believed that we who came from Bosnia to the federal authorities should not be sitting there in the federal authorities. He thought instead it was our duty, our moral duty, to go to our native territory. So by the nature of things I was supposed to go to Bosnia to place myself at the disposal of the Bosnian authorities and assume responsibilities that fall within the purview of the Bosnian SUP. It was not a voluntarily departure, and I must confess that the way I was sent was something I didn't find very appropriate, but I could do nothing about it. I don't have the right to refuse an order by my superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in terms of your -- your service with the federal SUP for this assignment, you were told to go on vacation but while you were in Bosnia, or in the RS, you were -- you continued to be paid by the federal SUP and that counted toward your retirement in the federal SUP?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was an employee of the federal SUP and that was never in question. But to make things look more authentic, we were not going there as members of the federal SUP. They were sending us there as volunteers and we received formal decisions on annual leave, whereas, we were in fact officially sent to Bosnia and Herzegovina and I had all the authorisations and papers and everything as a member of the federal SUP. And an according to the legislation prevailing then, we had powers on the territory of every republic, if we were on official mission there. But we were sent there as volunteers and we were represented as volunteers because we left our federal IDs behind and we received new IDs upon arrival there and we became officially policemen of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In -- in terms of trying to narrow down the date when this occurred, I'd like to show you an exhibit. This is Exhibit P1144. Mr. Davidovic, in preparing for your testimony today, did you have occasion to listen to a number of intercepted telephone conversations?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Several conversations were played to me, listening to some of them I was alone. When I listened to others, there were some other people present, and I reviewed all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This first one is one dated the 6th of May, 1992, with Pero Mihajlovic and he is talking to a person he calls Comrade Secretary. Do you know who the other speaker in that conversation was?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's the federal minister; that is the federal secretary --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who is informing him of our arrival in Republika Srpska. That's the date when we got there. And after that date came the conversation marked 43 here. It says it was the 6th of April but it could only have been later because only after that conversation, when our federal secretary was informed did this other conversation with Kertes occur. I think I explained this to you during proofing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You did, thank you. I think the interpreter didn't catch the name of the federal secretary. Could you repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Pero Mihajlovic was talking to the federal secretary of the interior, Petar Gracanin, who was a colonel-general and that's how we addressed him, comrade general. He was one of the veterans of the national liberation war, a member of the partisan movement and decorated as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This telephone call, Mr. Mihajlovic says he is in Vrace and that you Mico Davidovic, Deputy Commander of the brigade, were with him. If I understand what you are saying correctly, this is a visit you made to the RS before the meeting with Kertes and Gracanin when you were ordered to volunteer and take a group to go help the RS; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I just clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, if you could take a look at another one. This is Exhibit P1125. This is another telephone -- intercepted telephone conversation in which you are listed as one of the speakers. And the date indicated is 17 May 1992. Did you have a -- is this one of the ones you listened to?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Could you give us a reference to the tab number?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, this is tab 11.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I listened to that conversation. It's a conversation between me and Mr. Stanisic when I had already arrived in Sarajevo and when I called to say that I was there, that I am settled in my accommodation and that I was located in Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would this phone call have been after your conversation and the instruction from Kertes and Gracanin to volunteer and go to the RS?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. One more. Tab 12; Exhibit P1127. This is a phone conversation from -- from May but there's no -- no precise date indicated. Do you recall having listened to this conversation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you recognise the speakers listed, Mr. Gracanin and Mico Stanisic? Did you recognise their voices?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's what they told me. That's the conversation between Petar Gracanin and the minister of the interior of Republika Srpska, Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in their conversation one of the things that Gracanin talks about is having you go and report to General Mladic. Is that something you did when you were in the RS on that first trip, after you had been directed to go by Gracanin and Kertes?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well this conversation was about informing Mico Stanisic by Petar Gracanin that I was there, that I should go to General Ratko Mladic to report to him and to provide assistance if needed to him, because Petar Gracanin had spoken directly with General Mladic to say that I was coming, and I was directed to go to him with a request from Mico Stanisic, and this was also arranged between Petar Gracanin and Ratko Mladic in a previous conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: While we're looking at intercepts, let me do one last one and we'll be done with those.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we have a look at tab 73. This is 65 ter number -- oh, I'm sorry, it's Exhibit P1131.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall having listened to this one during your proofing?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you recognise the voice of Mr. Stanisic on that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you see that the -- the other speaker is listed as Nedjelko Zugic. Do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I clarified that straight away. I don't know who this Nedeljko Zugic is. As far as I remember, if that's the one, there was one Zugic who was from Olivo. I think he was Crisis Staff commander or something like that. I'm not quite sure, if that's the Zugic you mean. And I know that he was involved later in a scandal with shipments of cigarettes and liquor to areas inhabited by Muslims and there was some trade going on, something like that. If that is that man. I'm not even sure who -- which Zugic it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now return to your statement. And after you got the direction to go on vacation and take yourself to the Republika Srpska, you tell us in your statement that you and your colleagues flew to Belgrade -- from Belgrade to Pale by a helicopter. And then from Pale you went in five Pinzgauers to Vrace when and where did you meet Mico Stanisic when you went on this first trip?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: When we were sent to Republika Srpska, we flew out from Batajinica by helicopter to Pale. There was sports centre with a large field belonging to some local club. And then we went down to the base which was the station, the base of the local MUP and that's where Mico Stanisic was based and that was in fact the training centre at Vrace. That was the headquarters of the Ministry of Interior. And upon arriving there, I did not immediately meet with Mico. I think it was only into my third day there that we met very late at night around 11 p.m. I told him I was settled there, and after that, Petar Gracanin was given a telephone call to be told that I was there. That was my first encounter with Mico Stanisic in the locality of Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Had you known Mico Stanisic before this occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew Mico from earlier on. He worked for the Ministry of Interior, but I personally met him when I was on that commission of the federal SUP, and we visited the Security Services Centres, inter alia, Sarajevo, and that's when I met Mico. I cannot confirm exactly what his position was, whether he was the deputy head of the Sarajevo centre or the chief of the service. I know that we came across him in the office and he told us about the problems in the area covered by the centre of Sarajevo. That's when I met him for the first time. I think that we saw each other again after that, but that was our first official meeting and the first time we met, and that is what I remember. At that time, there was still a single SUP of the BH and Minister Delimustafic held that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you met Mr. Stanisic in Vrace, what conversation, if any, did you have with him about why you were there and what you were supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was a brief conversation, by way of information, in terms of whether we had found accommodation. We briefly inquired how many people there were and what should be done. And then I was briefly told that my role and function would be to help constitute their special unit that was then partly put up in Vrace and it consisted in part from the former special unit that was stationed in the area of the school in Vrace and we were supposed to try to establish a special unit and train it for special tasks that would be put before it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you actually able to do that? And tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was hard to do anything at the time, and that quickly at that. When we arrived there, I think that 12 people were singled out from the special unit that had existed until then. It was either nine or 12. I don't know why I confuse the two figure but I keep confusing them all the time. Then these people came and we reached agreement in principle with the commander of that unit. At that time, it was Karisik down there. Repija had been wounded and he was transferred to Belgrade and he was hospitalised at the VMA. We had agreed that those members of the special unit who were down there and who had undergone this training would take ten members of the reserve force, and then with one of our men and with one of their former members of the special forces, I mean, very often this term is being used for people who have nothing to do with the special forces and who are not trained adequately, or whatever, but they say that they are. And they tried to work with these people on a day-to-day basis to make sure that they can protect themselves, that they know how to use weapons, that they know how to take up certain premises. Well, this is how I speak. I cannot speak fast -- I cannot speak slower and I cannot speak more loudly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry, I was giving you a signal to slow down because it looked like the interpreters were requesting that. All right. We saw earlier in the intercept between Mico Stanisic and Mr. Gracanin, there was a -- talk about you reporting to General Mladic. In paragraph 54 of your statement - that's page 14 of the English - I'm not sure which page of the B/C/S paragraph 54 is. You talk about going to Lukavica Barracks and a meeting you had there with General Mladic and Radovan Karadzic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did not go to report to Ratko Mladic. That wasn't my duty to report to Ratko Mladic. He was not my superior officer. I was actually sent by my own minister, the federal minister, Petar Gracanin to report to Ratko Mladic. Now why was I supposed to call on Ratko Mladic? First of all, if I need more equipment, arms, ammunition, any kind of equipment because at the time it was still the federal army just like the federal SUP was still in existence. Whatever I needed I should ask General Ratko Mladic for. And in that way, I could get the equipment I needed and that was the main reason why I came to pay this visit to General Ratko Mladic. When I actually came to General Ratko Mladic, there was another general in his office. I think he was a Montenegrin. I know later on that he was commander of the Drina Corps in the area in Bajina Basta, towards Skelani, Bratunac, Srebrenica, but I don't know exactly what his name is. I couldn't remember. A few minutes later, after about 10 or 15 minutes, Mr. Radovan Karadzic walked into this room where General Mladic was. As he walked in I took advantage of that to inform General Ratko Mladic and Radovan Karadzic at the same time with a particular occurrence, namely that there was a great deal of looting that was being carried out by members of the reserve force and some informal groups that were milling about Vrace. They barged into other people's apartments, took away things from these apartments and then probably sold them somewhere, took them away. I asked for measures to be taken and for protection to be ensured and then when things were being seized by the polices they should be handed over at a particular place. And then I brought this up with General Mladic and at the same time, thereby, Karadzic as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your statement you indicated that in this discussion Mr. Karadzic said that while you should try to prevent looting, there should be no arrest of Serbs or conflicts between Serbs. Did General Mladic respond to that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: General Ratko Mladic spoke then as well. He said that some kind of central warehouses should be established and whatever was taken from persons, I mean, if something had been looted, if it was the result of a crime, that then all of these things should be given to families of fallen veterans. Radovan Karadzic also said that such looting should be prevented and that should disallowed. However, what we should pay attention to is that Serb should not take Serb, that a Serb should not draw weapon against a Serb, as it were, heaven forbid. So that there would not be a conflict between people of Serb ethnicity because that would be terrible and what would happen would be like what happened in the Second World War, that's exactly what he said. And that thesis went on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter did not understand the last part of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Davidovic, the interpreter indicates that they weren't able to hear the last part of your sentence of what you just said. Could you repeat that, if you recall what it was? It's after your reference to the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was saying that Radovan Karadzic insisted that a Serb should not shoot at a Serb or kill a Serb and that we should not go back to the Second World War when there was a clash between the partisans and the Chetnik. It was a conflict between the Serbs, actually the conflict between the partisans and the Chetniks. He meant that this should not happen again during this war, that war and that this should be prevented even if it were done at the expense of not punishing perpetrators of crimes. I have more to say about that, but I'll do it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then let me move to paragraph 58 of your statement. It's page 16 of the B/C/S and page 15 of the English. You say there that after this meeting at Lukavica Barracks with Mladic and Karadzic that Mr. Stanisic, Mico Stanisic, called you into his office at the Hotel Kikinkda at Pale and there were just the two of you, and you explained to him the situation as you saw it. What was the situation as you saw it? What did you explain to him at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The two of us talked and I said then to Minister Stanisic that I had seen that I had witnessed the organised looting of property, especially belonging to persons of Muslim ethnicity, that apartments were being broken into and that things were being carried out of these apartments. Also I asked him what these people were doing, these people who were driving around some Golf cars, part of the members of the Dusko Malovic's units. Where do these Golfs come from? What were they doing with them? Mico told me in respect of the first part and since there was a war going on things happened as they happened, and it was only natural that certain crimes were being committed and that we should work on preventing them. As for the Golfs and their driving them, they had the concent, or, rather, President Karadzic gave his concent to the Ministry of Interior that they could get the equipment that was indispensable for the Ministry of Interior at the time by selling these Golfs. I don't know. I have to repeated that, I don't remember whether it happened at that particular meeting but I think that it happened later. At another meeting, Mico offered me a Golf but I don't think it was that first time. I think it was around the second time when we were talking after the new developments that took place at the time. He asked me, Do you need a car? Is there any need for that, and I said there was no need and that ended that particular conversation so we didn't discuss it any further. I mean, I think there's a difference there. It wasn't during that first conversation that the Golfs were brought up. It was after a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Paragraph 62 you mention that you -- after this meeting -- paragraph 59, I'm sorry, after this meeting you and your staff were sent by Mr. Stanisic to Mount Jahorina to help secure the government officials and facilities. And in paragraph 62 you say that you stayed there for about ten days before you returned to Belgrade. Paragraph 62 is at page 16 of the English and page 17 of the B/C/S. You say that: "Prior to leaving, we were instructed to leave behind our weapons and equipment, including the five Pinzgauer and leave that with the new RS MUP special purposes units headed by Milenko Karisik." Who gave you that instruction to leave behind that equipment and weapons and vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'll go back to that other paragraph, 59. You mentioned something in relation to the meeting I had with Stanisic. And when Stanisic went to the Bistrica Hotel, when we went to provide security for the government. After staying at this school in Pale for about ten days we were sent to the lines at the Jewish cemetery. We spent two or three days there, I think, at that line, and then I established contact with Petar Gracanin, the federal minister, and I familiarised him with these details, and I was saying, What are we doing here? We were not sent here to go to the front line. We came with a certain duty and task to carry it out. And he agreed and he probably talked to Mico Stanisic, and after that we, as a unit, were sent to Jahorina to provide security for the government that was staying there in two or three hotels. I cannot remember exactly. It was hotel Jahorina and hotel Bistrica. And that's where the members of the government were, that's where they slept or where they were as an institution of Republika Srpska. When we stayed in the territory up at there at Jahorina, we had the opportunity of being right there where the government was and the government members were. And on several occasions I had contacts with Minister Gracanin and I received an order from him because I was only answerable to him, and he issued me the following order: That when we withdraw, we leave all the weapons and ammunition and equipment that we have with them, even the vehicles, the Pinzgauers, and that we hand all that over to their special unit, newly formed, and its commander Milenko Karisik. I think that Mico Stanisic knew about that as well. He wasn't there at the time that we were leaving, but I think that he knew we left our equipment to them because our Pinzgauers had licence plates and documents that indicated that they had belonged to the federal SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now at paragraph -- beginning at paragraph 64 to paragraph 101 of your statement, you talk a lot about the situation in Bijeljina. And after you returned to Belgrade, after this first visit, when you left behind your equipment and the Pinzgauers, how long did you stay in Belgrade before you were asked to return again to the RS, approximately, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think about a month, but please don't take my word for it. I know that we came again in the second half of July to Bijeljina and the difference was -- well, May, June, it could have been a month, and then in the second half of July I arrived Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before you had returned to Belgrade on that first occasion, had you made a trip to Bijeljina during your first stay?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who did you go with on that trip?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The first time I went from Pale to Bijeljina, I went with a group of members of my unit. At the time, from Njegus, from the Ministry of the Interior, I got some passports. I think -- well, I can't remember exactly. There could have been about up to 2.000 passports. I took them over and I handed them over to the Ministry of the Interior in Bijeljina, and they issued me a certificate. When I arrived Bijeljina, I found Pajo -- I mean Pejo not Pajo, some kind of a self-styled general, whatever he was, belonging to Arkan. And then I found Sasa and some other persons and they were staying there at the SUP, but they came considerably earlier, the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you. There I think it's almost time for our first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I have a question here. I was wondering, on your witness list -- on your list of documents, there 's indication that you would take 20 minutes for your examination-in-chief. On your list for witnesses for the week of 23 August, for this week, it says two hours. Where did it go from 20 minutes to two hours? I have a decision -- the Trial Chamber decision of 19 March, 2010, saying 20 minutes. Did that change in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think it changed and we were allowed an additional 2 hours and 40 minutes for a total of 3 hours. And I'm sorry that it says 20 minutes on there, but I was advised, and when checking, we had made a request to change his status from viva voce to 92 ter. The initial decision was 20 minutes and we'd asked fro additional time in the subsequent filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Shall we check that on both sides during the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But can I just add before we adjourn that the idea behind granting additional time beyond the 20 minutes for 92 ter witnesses was to allow for the calling party to introduce new evidence over and above what was already contained in his statement, and so far it looks to me as if we have been systematically going through the witness's 92 ter statement and so nothing new has come up so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So where did the additional time -- what is the basis for the additional time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Two things in regard, Your Honour. I'm trying -- I have to repeat some of what is said there just to locate him in the point where I'm asking the question. Then I am trying to ask for elaboration or clarification about what is actually said in the statement. In addition, the portions of his statement where he speaks directly about his contacts with Mico Stanisic I think need to be addressed live somewhat. Because I know this has been raised in other cases that even though he is here for cross-examination, to the extent it goes directly to the acts and the conduct of the accused, there's a preference that that be lead life. But if Your Honours are satisfied with what is in there, I can shortcut a lot of this, and I sense that is where you are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. And that's where the Rules are. Because the purpose of 92 ter is to save time by just admitting the 92 ter statement and then allowing for the Defence to cross-examine directly on the basis of that so we don't need to go through the earlier statements. It is really a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I hear you, Judge. I -- acting on my experience in another case with another Judge. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we will take the break now and resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, while the witness is being escorted back in, we have, during the break, been able to be reminded of our decision of the 8th of June, on the application of the Office of the Prosecution to be allowed additional time to introduce new material, and the result of that decision was, as I said, for the reasons advanced by its motion at the time, was to allow the Prosecution a total of two-hours to deal with this new material. The -- yes, so a total of two hours. And we are -- in other words so it is two hours, not three hours. And as I said, the purpose of that decision was for the admission of material that was outside of what would have been in the witness's previous statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we are holding you to that decision of two hours, and we expect that in the remaining 48 minutes, I believe it is, that you would -- yes, the Registrar has confirmed that. That in the remaining 48 minutes that you would use it as it was intended to introduce new material, and not, as Judge Harhoff said before the break, to spend the time just emphasising or highlighting portions of the previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I researched it as well and found the June 8 decision. My mistake was I think the Prosecution's application had been to ask for three. We were awarded an additional 1:40 for a total of two. I made a mistake when I asked someone to check and I was informed it was three instead of two. I will proceed and try to finish well within my remaining 48 minutes. I will, on occasion, be going to a couple of things in the statement where I am trying to get a little further answer to something that is in there and I may ask something that is there just to put him in context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: we understand that. But, of course, within your 48 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Understood. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, I want to -- I want to move now a little faster than I've been going. We are well covered because your prior testimony and your prior statement, I anticipate, will be in evidence. Paragraph 125, which is at page 131 of the English in your B/C/S statement, you talk about Arkan being controlled by the Serbian MUP, and you mentioned that Mico Stanisic went to that training camp, had been amazed to see how well it was run and the respect Arkan received from his men. I wanted to ask you, how did you know that Mico Stanisic went to Erdut? What was your source of information about that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I heard about that from Mico Stanisic because I saw him a day before that. He said that he would go to Erdut on the next day to visit Arkan's camp and that I would see him the next day after he comes back from the camp. And when I did see him, when he saw how all that had been equipped he was pleased and thrilled by everything that he seen there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you have any conversation with Mr. Stanisic about the presence of Arkan and his men and what they were doing in Bijeljina, Brcko, and the other territories where they had been seen in action in -- in the RS?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I did not elaborate on that with him. There was no need. From day one, even before the outbreak of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, people knew about it. Arkan came to Bijeljina. He did what he did there. He committed a series of crime, murders, robberies, that was repeated several times already. I don't see there's any need to discuss it any further. Anything he did, he did with the consents and control of the people from the MUP of Serbia. Primarily, Frenki and Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was Mico Stanisic aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I assume he was. He could not have not known, especially because he received information from several sources. General Mladic himself was against these members. There were quite a few complaints in respect of their behaviour and it was well-known what they were doing. He was appointed minister later and he probably had had insight into everything that was going on. He had the media there as well and had every opportunity to learn about all of that a lot earlier. Also, he occasion to encounter those people of his there. They moved about freely without any restraints. They had full freedom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you ever ask him why he wasn't taking any action against Arkan and his men?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when we talked when I came with the intention of disarming the paramilitaries, I was told then that quite simply they could not have opposed them. After all, they came under the guise of some kind of patriots to take part in this defence war as they called. However, very soon, they turned into their very contradiction, first when Arkan's Men came and then these others who introduced themselves as some kind of free fighters or some kind of patriot, usually they would first report to the Crisis Staffs. They provided all the necessary logistics to them, food, accommodation, et cetera, however usually these paramilitary formations, after a certain period of time, once they got to know the terrain, they would refuse to go to the front line and would be located in the urban areas. They killed and looted. They, in this way, mistreated legal citizens, Muslims. They liquidated some of them and other they transferred across the Drina River, whatever they did they robbed them of their property, they sold it further on and accumulated certain material goods in Serbia and that was so wide spread. There was practicality no place where they were not staying.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to -- I want to turn to paragraph 150 of your statement, which is at page 37 of the English. And I'll have the B/C/S reference in a moment. From paragraphs 151 to 165 you talk about the situation in Bijeljina after August 1992. And you make a reference to some killings of Muslim families in Bijeljina, which you say was part of a plan to intimidate and drive most of the rest of the remaining Muslims out. The B/C/S page is page 39 for paragraph 150. And I want to show you tab 65. This is an exhibit in evidence, P1543. With the usher's help, I would like to hand you a hard copy because I want to direct you to a page that's sort in the middle. It's page 67 of the B/C/S and page 65 of the English. I put a sticky on the page there for you. Yes. On the right-hand page. This exhibit is part of a file from the regional prosecutor's office in Bijeljina, dated the 14th of April, 2005. The particular page I referred you to is a statement from Mico Stanisic that was provided in response to that investigation. And in the paragraph -- it's the fourth or the third paragraph of his statement, he's talking about the special detachment of Dusko Malovic's --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a moment, if I may. Your Honours, part of this documentation that the Prosecutor is now trying to show to the witness relates to events that are not covered by the indictment, and a statement by Mr. Stanisic is being used, although we don't know whether Mr. Stanisic is going to testify in his own case, so I think it is inadmissible to use his statements for any -- from any other proceedings until he decides whether he will testify in this trial. And there is also his interview given to the OTP, so we should look into whether there are legal possibilities for using such documents that haven't yet seen their epilogue in trials in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So perhaps it might be inappropriate to use them before this court. And I believe we've made a similar objection in a previous case, or my colleague made it. And the Trial Chamber instructed that such documents may be used only very cautiously unless they touch upon the subjects of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's an interesting proposition of the law. I would like to see some citation for that proposition. Your Honour, Mr. Stanisic made this statement the last part of it says: "I've written this statement with my own hand. I accept every word as my own and I signed it with my own hand. Signed Mico Stanisic." The original is a hand-written document. Now if the Defence want to challenge authenticity and say, That is not his, well that is one thing. But otherwise any of the arguments just made should go to the weight of this. This incident, I know, is not one of the scheduled killings in our indictment, it is one that the Prosecution sought to add at the time we did the amended indictment. That was denied, but I think in the decision it was indicated that the Prosecution could lead evidence about that for other purposes, such as showing a pattern, et cetera. Part of what I'm trying to do now is this particular statement has to do with some issues of credibility and identification of people holding certain positions at certain times, and I think it's entirely proper for me to go into it. It was noticed on the list and I don't think there's any issue that this is Mr. Stanisic's statement that he provided to the authorities in -- in -- in Bosnia during an investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In terms of separating the two issues, I suspected that the first part of Mr. Cvijetic's objection to which was the second part of your response, the answer would -- as you have indicated been the rule about similar fact evidence. But may we have a moment to deal with the other part of Mr. Cvijetic's objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I raise one other point in connection with that. You know last week we had an issue come up with an objection sort at the end of the Prosecution's presentation of evidence about something that was in the 92 ter package. Here this is a document that was listed in our exhibits to be used. There was no objection raised, even though I sent an e-mail to Defence last week and said, Please advise me if you have any objections to any of these so we can discuss it beforehand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, we would, of course, consider any authority that you have to put before the Chamber in support of your proposition that the -- as we understand your proposition to be, that the Prosecution could not put into evidence a statement made by the accused out of court prior to the commencement of these proceedings. But until such time as we have had a chance to consider whatever authorities you would wish to rely on to support that proposition, and, of course, until we are persuaded that we should accept such authority, we would permit Mr. Hannis to continue the -- along the course that he is pursuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, you see that paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I -- I would like to respond. May I refer to your decision in which you refused the expansion of the indictment to include the events which Mr. Stanisic writes about in this statement. So I believe it is in your own decision that we may not deal with these incidents that are not the subject of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, the -- the separate issue as I understand it, apart from the statement having been made by Mr. Stanisic about this -- facts outside of the indictment, the -- you may have been present last week when I confessed my own difficulty with the -- what is known in the -- in other systems as similar fact evidence. Nevertheless, it is a well-settled rule that such evidence is admissible although they touch on matters not specified in the indictment. The ordinary rule in criminal proceedings, of course, being that relevance is determined by the indictment. But similar fact -- the admissibility of similar fact is so well settled, that I don't know that we need trouble ourselves with -- with explaining the rules for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more thing, Your Honours. Of course we will comply with any decision you make, but I'm afraid we are going into the sphere of the rights of the accused to decide how he will defend himself and we are prejudging his decision. You said that the Statute guarantees his right that he remains silent and I believe we are introducing something through a back door even before he decided whether he will testify in his own case or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You may have observed, Mr. Cvijetic, that I tried to phrase the response to your objection about the statement made by Mr. Stanisic in such a manner as to not close the door to your seeking to persuade the Chamber that it should wholly disregard it at a later stage. And should it turn out that we are so persuaded by the authorities that you produce to support your proposition, we would, as trained Judges have the ability to expunge from our considerations any impressions that we may have formed, as a result of receiving the evidence. But, at this stage, it strikes us that it is such a novel proposition that we think the proper course is to allow Mr. Hannis to continue. As I said, it is open to you to return to the matter at the appropriate stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, returning again to that document, and what Mr. Stanisic says about how Dusko Malovic's unit came to be sent to Bijeljina, which he said was in order to protect the security of the citizens of Bijeljina, especially non-Serbs: "I issued an order to have a platoon led by Dusko Malovic sent to Bijeljina and put at the disposal and further use of the head of the public security station, Mico Davidovic and under the full control of the MUP senior staff [sic] Tomo Kovac and Cedo Kljajic who were staying in Bijeljina at the time ..." My first question to you is: Were you head of the public security station in Bijeljina in September 1992, or at any time in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't, and I believe the allegations in this statement are not correct. Although let's take it in order. I was never the head of the police station, especially not in the period when the unit of Dusko Malovic arrived, nor was Tomo Kovac in the SUP there, nor did he come to call or was appointed, nor was Cedo Kljajic appointed there. So I can't really understand what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall who was --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it might be important later. 40:8, I believe, the witness said the -- different about Cedo Kljajic being only appointed. Maybe can you clarify this with the witness, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, could you tell us what you were saying about Cedo Kljajic and being in Bijeljina in September 1992; if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the questions you're asking are out of context, so I can't get to all the details. To give you a complete answer I would have to go into a much broader explanation, but I'll try. When the decision was made for the MUP of Republika Srpska to be moved to Bijeljina, in this building of the MUP of Bijeljina, the first to come was Cedo Kljajic as an assistant or deputy to Mico Stanisic, and I believe Devedlaka also came. He was under-secretary for state security, that is the secret police. And they were the one who set up the interior authorities in Bijeljina. They were based in the building of the MUP and they started to work. And on one occasion when I came, if you want to hear this, together with Dragan Adnan, I found Cedo Kljajic typing on a typewriters filling in a driving licence with the reference to a motor vehicle that was seized from some people in Brcko, and I asked him, What are you doing? What kind of driving licence is this? And then he told me that he had received approval from the minister to do this, to support his family, to be able to work and live, that he had no other sources of income and that it was his legal right that he received, in order to be able to work, if that's what you wanted to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Concerning this statement Mr. Stanisic made about the killings of three families in Bijeljina in September 1992, allegedly by the Dusko Malovic group, did you ever have any conversation with Mico Stanisic about that and his connection, if any, to those events?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will inform you briefly. On one occasion I met with Mr. Stanisic in Sremska Mitrovica and Stanisic had some questions about why I talked to the investigators of the Tribunal, whether he was also interesting to them, whether I had given any statements and I said, Yes, I talked to them, they also asked about him and in that context, his activities concerning the disarming of paramilitaries in Zvornik and other places was also discussed. And as far as this family from Bijeljina is concerned, I said that question had not been asked and then he said, Please, don't place me in that context, because he doesn't want to get involved and he doesn't want me to place him in any context related to that. And that's the first time this families with mentioned with him. The name begins with an S; I can't remember the name of the family. That's the conversation that took place. And otherwise, since, in the first half of August I was in Bijeljina, we were disarming these paramilitaries, after that I went to Montenegro where I stayed in Plevlje to arrest the group led by Ceko Dacovic [phoen], and when I returned from Montenegro three months later I found Dusko Malovic in Belgrade, in the so-called Bosnian villa, and when I asked him, Dusko what happened, who killed those people there? Dusko said Drago Vukovic ordered it at that time. Drago Vukovic was the under-secretary of the secret police in Bijeljina, in the Bijeljina centre. And he led all the activities related to that, and that conversation that I had with Dusko Malovic happened without Mico Stanisic. He arrived later. He arrived with Frenki Simatovic to this Bosnian villa. They wanted to talk to me about something. However, when Frenki came, he asked me, Who gave you the right to arrest Red Berets in Bijeljina and we had -- we locked horns there. We almost -- it almost came to a fist fight. I left. After that, Mico Stanisic stayed behind and not a word was said about this family that is mentioned in his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will stop there and see what I need to deal with on re-direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning Witness.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Once you have answered this question to Mr. Hannis, I don't think you gave a complete answer, and the question was: Were you able to place Mr. Stanisic in any context related to these events?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I said I didn't and I couldn't. I thought I was going answer Mr. Hannis to this question in paragraph 150. He asked me about the implementation of the policies of the Crisis Staffs in Bijeljina related to the ethnic cleansing in Bijeljina and the killing of Muslims but I didn't give that answer because Mr. Hannis moved to another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, in addition to the caution that Mr. Hannis would have given you about slowing down your replies to allow interpretation, this is especially important during cross-examination by Mr. Cvijetic, and in turn counsel for Mr. Zupljanin. Because you speak the same language, you have to remember to allow a gap between the question, an interval, between the question and your response so the interpretation may flow smoothly. Thank you. Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I'll try.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, I hope you don't mind I'll have to ask you to repeat your answer and I will repeat the question, just in case. So the question was: Then or now or at any time were you able to associate Mr. Stanisic in any way with this crime, the killing of the Sarajlic family, and please repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was not able to associate Mr. Stanisic with that killing in any way, because, as far as this killing is concerned and the other killings in Bijeljina are concerned, that took place before Mico Stanisic became head of that ministry and I also believe that Mico Stanisic didn't even know about that killing, because in this local part of the ministry it was being covered up because when this family was found murdered, somebody from the municipal authorities ordered that these corpses be thrown into the water so that the river may carry them away. That's what I heard. So there is no statement or interview where I was able to mention Mico Stanisic as in any way associated with this crime this Bijeljina. I think that's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I already objected to Mr. Hannis's dealing with this topic but I want to finish this. Are you able to associate Mr. Stanisic with this local policy or local politics and the people who conducted that policy?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I can't, because that all happened and all started before Mr. Stanisic came to be the head of the police. It started when the SDS came into power in Bijeljina and started to establish themselves and their government in terms of ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Give me just a yes-or-no answer. Are you able to associate him with that kind of policy at the local level?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he wasn't there at the time. He couldn't be associated with that in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's finish with this topic. Let's then go back to your early days. I'll follow your statement in parallel with your testimony in the Krajisnik case and compare, but don't hold it against me if I look at the papers too much, but I hope I'll finish within the allocated time. You claimed and you continue to assert that after the multi-party elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina you personally did not accept the offer to join the Serbian Democratic Party; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You stated as the main reason that you did not accept the idea that political parties should be organised as national parties.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that there existed also a legal reason why you, as a policeman, could not be a member of a political party or involved in politics.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: These regulations, I believe, still do not permit policemen to be involved in politics because the two activities are incompatible.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That was so then, and it is so now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, just to be totally clear on this, in your first question, at that time, you asked about a policeman -- you said, "... a policeman could not be a member of a political party or be involved in politics." And the witness answers, "yes." And then still for the -- for the -- at this moment, it is not permitted for policemen to be involved in politics. Answer: Yes. Does that also mean still at this time that policemen cannot be member of a political party, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Policemen could never be members of political parties or be involved in politics. That was the case before the war and it is still law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
