utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Davidovic, I looked at the Law on Internal Affairs of the then Socialist Republic Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I found that there existed a legal possibility, and that was followed in practice, in fact, that members of the ministry, which was not called ministry at the time, it was scald the Secretariat for Internal Affairs, they could be transferred to the Federal Secretariat for Internal Affairs. I don't want to show that piece of legislation to the Trial Chamber. Just confirm that it is so.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely correct. The federal SUP was in fact constituted from staff from various republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm more interested in another thing which I believe is more relevant to your testimony here. There is an reverse option also, as a member of the Federal Secretariat for Internal Affairs could be transferred on a legal, profession mission to the territory of another republic and to legally carry out your work for which you are authorised. And not to waste time, I will immediately show you that you piece of legislation to see if I found the right article which enabled you to be transferred to Republika Srpska Bosnia-Herzegovina as you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I call up P530.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly which page it is, but Article ought to help. I'll give you the number of the Article.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just let me see ... A correction, please. It's P530. And we need Article 64, 65, and 66. In the B/C/S version it is most probably page 10; and in the English version it is page 11. Or the other way around. English page 10; Serbian, 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English version, it's page 10. In the Serbian version, it's page 9; I'm sorry. We see in the English version the appropriate page. We still don't have the Serbian version. Yes, there it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, I would like to ask you to look at the Articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can they please enlarge Articles 64, 65, and 66 in the B/C/S version for you, please. Yes, that's it. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me just add that this is the Law on Internal Affairs adopted by Republika Srpska. And let me just add that I have compared it with the Law on Internal Affairs by the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and they are completely identical. So would you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... object to Mr. Cvijetic testifying about what some document that he hasn't shown the witness says. That's something that he can submit to Your Honours at the end of the case, but that is not something that he should present to the witness without showing it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have presented the documents, the relevant provisions. I just want to ask the witness about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me just put this question to you, sir. On the basis of these precisions, can you understand it in the sense that you were authorised to Republika Srpska or Bosnia and Herzegovina and to carry out the assignments that are mentioned here, even though you were part of the federal ministry?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree. But I would like to add an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll let the witness finish his answer, but I would like to object because this witness was not a member of the police in the Republika Srpska. He was a member of the police in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. This law applies to not his country, and Republika Srpska was not part of the FRY at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is not my intention to elaborate a lot about the elements mentioned by Mr. Hannis because it's not relevant for this witness. But I can say in response to the comment of Mr. Hannis, and it's not my intention to testify, the answer can be found in the constitution of Republika Srpska. But I would just like to ask the witness to read the Article 66 where it is stated that upon arrival in the territory of Republika Srpska he would have all the authorities of police members of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The Article speaks for itself. We don't need the witness to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, the witness can read the Article and Mr. Cvijetic can frame a question. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'll put a direct question to you. Could you please answer with yes or no. As a member of the Federal Secretariat of the Interior, could you come to Republika Srpska or Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and carry out certain assignments, yes or no? There is no need for explanation.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I cannot give you a yes-or-no answer. This is an answer that requires a proper answer. Since you're asking me, I did have the rights and authorities as you put to me, but according to earlier constitution and the Law on Internal Affairs, the federal SUP had the instructional overview rights and they were then transferred to republics. We did not have rights or authorities except the State Security Service, of course, but if there was general interest or common interest in carrying out joint actions that needed to be done jointly, and to work together, then a mixed or joint team would be sent, and, for instance, we would come there to see if there were any violations of laws before the war. That was the right of the relevant federal SUP. It's not like in the federal police of the United States where they could -- where they can come at any -- to any area and do whatever they want. We could not do that. That was not part of the federal authority, because republics were autonomous in carrying out their internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for the explanation. I will not put any further questions in relation to that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, may I ask one clarification. When you put -- put the question to the witness: "As a member of the Federal Secretariat of the Interior, could you come to the Republika Srpska or the republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and carry out certain assignments, yes or no?" When you asked "certain assignments," do you mean assignments by the Federal Secretariat of the Interior, or do you mean assignments by the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that was precisely what I had asked the witness to explain, what kind of assignments he could come and assist with, and I think we did receive an answer from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Well, no, we didn't receive a clear answer to that. So my question would be: Are we talking about assignments given by the -- the federal authorities or are we talking about assignments given to a federal -- member of the Federal Secretariat of the Interior given by the Republika Srpska? Mr. Witness? In fact, I should put the question to -- to Mr. Zecevic [sic] because I want to know, what he is looking for, what his question is. The question isn't clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It -- I would only -- the only thing I could do is put the question again to the witness and maybe assist him by saying: To what kind of tasks were you sent or arrived to carry out? Were it those of common interest where one could find link between federal and republic level.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a better question although it still requires a longer answer. I did not come in accordance to this Article that you've produced to me. In testimony in Krajisnik case, I explained this. I came based on a request issued by the organs of Republika Srpska, most probably the ministry, although Karadzic in his conversations with Mr. Panic who was president of the federal government and they had these talks in, I think, Geneva, and Karadzic then explained that he is not able to fight against paramilitary formations that had come from Serbia, and then Mr. Panic, who was the prime minister of Serbia and Montenegro, offered some of the federal SUP forces to help with the disarmament of these paramilitary formations. It was a political agreement between Republika Srpska and the prime minister at the time, Mr. Panic. And on the basis of this, I received a legal order. I reported to the Ministry of the Interior, told Mr. Stanisic I was at his disposal. I had the authority to disarm the paramilitary formations. I hope my answer was clear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it clear now, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It is clear now. I would have hoped it would have been clear with your question, but the witness's answer is clear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Since, in your answer to the Honourable Judge, you spoke about paramilitary formations. Let me show you document P591. Mr. Davidovic, as you can see, this is a report on paramilitary formations in the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The author of this report, as can you see, is the Main Staff department for intelligence and security affairs. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please look at this first page. I'm not going to ask you about too many details. There's only one segment of this report that I'm interested in. Have you looked at it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You've seen what the purpose of this report is, what are the main elements related to paramilitary formations. And what I'm interested in can be found on the third page of this document in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the third page of the B/C/S. I'm interested in the second and the third paragraph there. Let me just see where's the appropriate page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, as can you see, the report deals with individual groups. There's mention of Yellow Wasps, Zute Ose. Apparently there is 170 of them. Furthermore, we have the further mention --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Red Berets and so on, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: According to your estimate, is this a realistic number of people in these units?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the factual situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So let's discuss this just in principle instead of going into details. This shows the actual situation in Republika Srpska at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Davidovic, you will agree with me that the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska, in order to deal with such numerous paramilitary formations needed support of all structures and communities of Republika Srpska; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In your statement, and also during the testimony, you stated that Mr. Stanisic, indeed, had a special unit but that they didn't have sufficient number of troops, nor were they trained well enough to properly, without assistance, deal with paramilitary formations and their crimes. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And that was one of the reasons why you arrived in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My first arrival was in order to train the special units; and my second time, my second visit, was for the purpose of arresting these paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You stated that you assisted with organisational formation of the special unit, however that did you not have time to provide a detailed training; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course. They were not trained at all. That was obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Was that the reason why you had certain reserves concerning their involvement in the operation aimed at Yellow Wasps?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see them as a unit that fit to do a task such as this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: However, you do say that they managed to do their part of the task and reach the seat of the Yellow Wasps, together with your units and that, in a way, they did do their job; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. But what they did was a marginal part of the assignment. I didn't give them an assignment that was of any great importance. That was my purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Davidovic, the order and the authorisation for this operation was issued by Mr. Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This was a very secret action. It was conducted secretly?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, completely secretly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You received full authority to plan and carry out this operation in operative sense; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: At the time of the preparations for this operation, you had also information that the members of the said unit, in addition to being involved in classical, typical, regular crime, were also involved in crimes against civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen that personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The operation received its approval without any restrictions. The task of the operation was to uncover any kind of criminal acts, no matter what they may be.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I told you about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: As for the prosecution of war crimes, it was the military prosecution organs and the military organs of the judiciary that were in charge, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. An explanation is required, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Was that the reason why the unit of the military police took part in it, if I'm not mistaken. You may clarify that now, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think that this answer needs to be explained a bit more. During the planning of the action, I found out that, in addition to grave crimes, robbery, murder, et cetera, I found out that in Celopak, the Muslims were taken and detained at the community centre and some of them were even killed. I came about this information when I went out to reconnoitre, to see how I could go to Zvornik and how I could overcome this paramilitary formation and deal with everything that they had done. Then I went to Han Pijesak with the intention of meeting with Tolimir, the chief of security of the Army of Republika Srpska. When I talked to him, he told me that he knew what was going on in Zvornik, and for that reason he said that within the activity of my unit the military security should take part as well. So Petar Salapura, a high-ranking security officer from the ranks of the Republika Srpska, was involved, together with me, in the planning of this action that we carried out together, with his security officer, yet another one who later on took over the entire situation of the war crimes, the entire case of war crimes, he actually took statements and was involved in the prosecution of war crimes, in addition to those grave crimes that I had already referred to, robbery, murder, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I think that we have come to a point when I should show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D75 it is. And I would like to have that document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We will deal with this document briefly. As I followed your testimony in the Krajisnik case, I realised that you had been shown this document. You are aware of this information, this document. You saw it right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, the second page, Macar signed it, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is very brief and this information is very brief and only the very basic details have been written up here. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You said then, and I'm just going to repeat the question, does it actually faithfully reflect how the action developed, although it is rather brief and --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly, it does reflect the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just move to the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Davidovic, what you stated is actually written here, and it says that there is one person who is a war crime suspect and that he was handed over to the military organs for further prosecution. That's what you know and that is what is written here. Is what is written here correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was transferred to the military garrison, to the military police in Bijeljina. Actually, I saw a document somewhere. Now I don't know whether it was a document that came from you or from the OTP. I think that it was a military security captain who took a statement from him, but now I cannot recall who it was that showed me this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not sure what the right time for a break would be. I have just prepared this document for the witness so that we could deal with it. So would that be all right? Oh, it is all right. Okay. Then we are going to deal with 1D39 -- actually, it's been given a new number. It received a new number the other day. It is actually P, P1539. It's a Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The print is very small, so can he just have a look at it? Can it be zoomed in so that he would see whether that is the statement that he referred to?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the statement that I had referred to. It's from the military police and that's the statement that was given to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. You said what you worked on. You worked on general crime. You wrote up the criminal report. And you started the relevant proceedings before the court in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We arrested the person. We submitted criminal report concerning grave crimes that were committed in Zvornik, and the military security dealt with the evidence concerning war crimes. Now, I know that proceedings were started, but I cannot be sure about the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. I will complete this by dealing with an unfinished topic from the Krajisnik case. You do remember that this was accompanied by rumours that the police had been involved in some kind of abuse and that more gold had been taken than had been registered. You explained what happened. Remind me. You said it was locked in a safe or something? In the Bijeljina Security Services Centre when you were leaving after that action; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Ministry of Interior had left everything there. There were vehicles that had been seized and there was gold. I cannot remember, it was like a kilogram and a half or so. I cannot remember. Also, there was also some gold jewellery there. We seized that and stored it with the Ministry of Interior, and I had an Official Note stating that and who received all of these goods at the Bijeljina MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, according to the Law on Criminal Procedure and according to the rules provided by the minister concerning such deposits, if the seized goods were not the object of a crime, then, according to the law, they have to be returned to the rightful owners; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the law says.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, if I have enough time, I would like to show you a document, but I believe that it may be a good idea to take the break now, Your Honours, because I would like to show him a document that has to do exactly with this topic that I have just dealt with now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is it going to take you longer than five minutes? Because we're five minutes away from the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It won't. I'm going to finish with this document within five minutes. P317, item 20. I have to repeat, P317, item 20. I give the 65 ter number, 2729, just in case. So whatever is easier for you, in order to be able to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- you are aware this is a confidential document, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, now I do know. Then we'd have to move into private session so that the witness could give his comments with regard to what he sees. That would be all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And we take the break, to resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You may continue, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, before we continue, I said I had to follow in parallel your statement in the Krajisnik case. You said a moment ago, and it's your statement as well. Let me give a reference. It's paragraph 65 of your statement. You can open it to see that, on one occasion, you walked in on Cedo Kljajic when he was filling in a vehicle permit form for his own needs. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Before I ask you the actual question. Can you please confirm that during our interview, I showed you a binder full of orders, instructions, and measures taken by the ministry to elucidate the Volkswagen Golf affairs and scandals. Can you just confirm you saw these documents?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now in the light of what you've seen, do you allow for the possibility that Mr. Cedo Kljajic, when he referred to Mr. Stanisic, just covered himself. In fact, he was lying?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer because it overlapped with the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry before we --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I allowed the possibility, everyone has the right to lie. Certainly he seemed surprised when I walked in on him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I would appreciate if counsel would stop when he sees me rising to raise an objection. Secondly, Your Honour, I have an objection because it is my understanding that when Defence counsel saw the witness yesterday it was just the two of them. Now he is asking about all these documents I showed you, did that change your mind or cause to you allow for the possibility that what you say about Mr. Kljajic here is a result of Mr. Kljajic lying. We don't know what documents he showed the witness. I don't have them, I don't know how many there are. I don't know if they are authentic. I don't know anything about them and neither do you. And we -- it is not an appropriate way to proceed. He should have another witness [sic] present when he is cross-examined and when he is interviewing a witness like that, in case the witness contradicts him, otherwise he puts himself in the position of making himself a witness in the case in which he's an advocate; and secondly, we don't know what those documents are and whether I can't cross-examine the witness now about whether that is a legitimate basis for you to change their mind. Because I don't know what they are, how many, or if they are authentic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, the bundle of objections which Mr. Hannis has just articulated, the -- what is your response? Because the reason why I refer is to a bundle of objections is there are a number of issues which your question and the manner in which you phrase your question have raised, even -- certainly in my mind even before Mr. Hannis would have articulated his objection, and my concern is that the set-up, as it were, for the question, is such that I don't know what use we could make of the answer when all of this is -- at the end of the exercise. What is your response?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my response is very simple. That issue was raised both in direct examination, and it is dealt with in the witness statement. And the documents I've shown him regarding all the operations of the Ministry of Interior to elucidate this Golf scandal is already part of the evidence. I did not find it necessary to bring the entire binder and show the documents one by one here. Some of these were unfamiliar to the witness, and he didn't even know that such orders were made. That's how I set the legal groundwork for my question. If I made a mistake when asking this last question, whether he allowed for the possibility that Mr. Kljajic was lying, I'm sorry. If I had brought the binder to deal with it here it would take an hour at least, and we've seen it, and we've gone through it at least ten times in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That is not the point, as I appreciate it. Certainly you are able, Mr. Cvijetic, to phrase a question that the witness can readily answer, albeit that the background would have been this bundle of documents without putting the documents in. But I have a problem with questions such as do you allow for the possibility that somebody is lying. You know, what assistance, what possible assistance to the Chamber could there be from any answer that such a question elicits?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, and I will try not to use this method any further in this witness's examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation], Mr. Davidovic, let us look at paragraph 58 of your statement. Earlier today, responding to a question from Mr. Hannis, you said Mr. Stanisic offer add vehicle to you and I'm not going make any more introductions. I was already wrapped on the knuckles for that. I will just say that he offered you -- that's what you say in the statement, he offered you and your men one Volkswagen Golf. Did that actually mean you could have a car issued to you officially?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't mention and I cannot qualify whether it was offered on a private or an official basis. When he mentioned this Volkswagen Golf vehicle, I said without any further adieu that we don't need it, we have our own vehicles and equipment. And that was the end of the conversation. In my mind, there was no need to go on about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will seek no further clarification. Let us move to paragraphs -- to paragraph 114. Look at the bottom of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 10472; that's the witness statement. Paragraph 114. Page 30 in Serbian -- no. It's page 30 in English and page 31 in Serbian. Fine. I expect the other version will also be displayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Look at the bottom of that paragraph 114 where you said that Mr. Andan quarreled with Mico Stanisic and that Mr. Stanisic criticised Mr. Andan, because, I quoted: "He was too kindly disposed towards Muslims." Now does this phrasing in your statement reflect exactly what you said? Could you explain a little.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think I owe you an explanation. When I went to Sarajevo, and when it was agreed that he should come with his unit to Bijeljina to disarm -- that we should come to Bijeljina to disarm paramilitaries, the issue arose who would be the co-ordinator between me, the unit and the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska, and that's when Cedo Kljajic said that Dragomir Andan should be co-opted or seconded to us. Until then, I had never heard of the man. I just heard of him as an employee of the Ministry of Interior. I heard -- I was told that he was in Brcko. He wasn't busy with anything special and that he was available to us. That's when Mr. Stanisic said, Who is this Dragomir Andan, why he is in Brcko? Then the other one said I invited him and then he said in rather brutal terms, I don't need a man like that here. Where are those Muslims now? Where is that Macar? I can't remember the name, was it Mujo or something. But anyway it was mentioned that Dragan Andan was also a football referee in his private life and that's how they knew him and that's probably the reason why Mico Stanisic said what he said. And he said, Don't worry, he will be able to do that work and that's how this whole conversation between me, Cedo and Mico ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You explained that, as a football referee he received meat from a butcher as a bribe and that's the point?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what exactly it was about but some butcher was mentioned and this sort of corruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Could you just finish your answer. You said -- or he said, I don't need that kind of man?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he said, I don't need that kind of man. He was opposed to his coming, and I even thought he issued an order to that effect; but, later, the man did come, at the insistence of Cedo Kljajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So how did he turn out to be in carrying out this work with you in Zvornik, Bijeljina, Brcko?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: He turned out to be quite good. He was very energetic, professional, qualified policeman. I was able to rely on him completely, whatever assignment I gave him he performed it impeccably, and I must say that I have a very high opinion of him as a police officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could we just clarify the meaning of your testimony here? Did you understand Mr. Stanisic's comment on Dragan Andan to be that Andan would not be a qualified person because he was just a football referee. Was that the reason why Stanisic didn't want him in this operation, according to your memory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I don't -- that's not what I meant. I don't think he thought that disqualified him, that he was a football referee in his private life. He wasn't thinking of Dragan Andan as a referee. I think it was all about something else. Mico Stanisic thought Dragan Andan to be a corrupted man, who was a corrupted referee with his own corrupted dealings in this football activity together with some other people, including that butcher. I think it was all about his opinion of Dragan Andan as a corrupt man. That's what I meant and that's what I understood Mico Stanisic to think of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So it had nothing to do with his being prejudiced -- his being too lenient with the Muslims, as your statement seems to suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Your Honours. I thought I heard one of the few B/C/S words I know spoken by the witness and not showing up in the English translation, which was "Muslimani," and I don't see anything about Muslims. I don't know if my B/C/S friends across the way heard the same thing, but if we could ask him about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe the witness should first answer your question because that was going to be my question, my next question.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I can quote, I remember it in detail and he said the following: Where are those Muslims to help Dragan Andan now? Where is that butcher? Where are his pork carcasses now, pork legs? I think he meant his character as a corrupt man, knowing about him from before, and I don't think that he thought he would be a welcome addition in that operation of disarming paramilitaries. I believe that it had to do with -- with his taking bribes, not his activity in sports and activity as a referee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I apologise for dwelling into this question. But, you see, in your statement, the implication that you seem to have raised was that Mr. Stanisic didn't like Mr. Andan because he thought that Mr. Andan was to well inclined towards Muslims. And so, therefore, the question is, directly to you here and now, was that your impression, or are we to understand your statement so as to mean that what Stanisic may have had against Mr. Andan had nothing to do with Mr. Andan's relations with the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally believe that the opinion of Mico Stanisic had to do only with the qualities of this person as a person. My view of Mico Stanisic is that he wasn't making any distinctions between Serbs and Muslims --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, of Dragan Andan that he wasn't making any distinctions between Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw him as a very responsible, professional person, that was my view of him. I don't know what the opinion of Mico Stanisic of this man was because of their previous experience. I think they had worked together earlier and maybe had some experiences between them. I had only heard about Dragan Andan, I hadn't met that person before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. This solves the issue, and you may move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Davidovic, let us complete this topic. Are you saying, then, that the position of Mr. Stanisic is not in any way related to the views Mr. Andan had in relation to Muslims in general, that Mr. Stanisic was speaking about a specific incident involving some Muslims and that he believed that he was not fit to carry out police tasks because of that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I just repeated what I heard from Mico Stanisic. I don't know what his views were. You must accept that. But let me add something. In later contacts with Mico Stanisic, I never made an impression that he has any specific position in relation to Muslims. I saw him as a man who is at high position, who insists on legality, and I don't believe he had any views about Muslims. And now if we're talking about the relationship between Andan and Stanisic, it was not an issue for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think everything is clear now. Let us go on. During your interview with the OTP, you gave them a document. They put this document at our disposal. It's D103-4841. I was told that it wasn't translated. Let me just clarify. Since we received this document last night we don't have a translation of it. And I would just like to ask the witness whether he can recognises the document he had handed over and then maybe explain what the document is and once we have the translation, we will ask for this document to be introduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D03-4841. I'm being told that the number is correct and that the document is in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, since we brought the document to the Prosecutor, there's no need for you to read it. Can you just tell us what it is. Could you just tell us what we can see in the heading?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just explain briefly. I got my hands on the document from the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska in relation to forming a commission that was ordered by Mico Stanisic. This commission was headed by Goran Macar and the task of the commission was to determine what has been taken out from the deposit of the Ministry of Interior who received what, what was done with these items and so forth. Having read the report, I found in the last or in the penultimate item, it's on the following page, I saw that Dragan Andan had seized a gambling machine. It's specified which precise gambling machine, that it was taken out of the safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It's on the last page of the document. Page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please find the last page of the document and show it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's item number 4 -- or, rather, page 4, second paragraph. It says here --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the 4th of July, 1992, this gambling machine was seized. You can see the name of it and it is stated also that the document [as interpreted] was allegedly not working, and it was taken out for some professional purpose. This is what I've read here and let me now explain why I handed over the document and why I find it of particular interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let us be more specific. Since we're dealing with Dragan Andan, if you allow me?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, but this is also related to Dragan Andan, so after having completed the arrest of the Yellow Wasps, there was a big cry-out among the political structures. People wanted me to be withdrawn from there and sent back. Since, in the meantime Pavle Bulatovic replaced Petar Gracanin as the federal minister, I was told to take my unit first to Belgrade and then to Montenegro, the area of Plevlje because there were also cases of violations by paramilitary formations, Ceko Dacovic and such. And then about 15 days after that, Dragan informed me that Mico Stanisic relieved him of duty, that he doesn't have a position at the time, that he is, in other words, without a job. And I wondered what had happened, why was he fired. And then, after so many year, I see this document where I can see that he has taken out this gambling machine which was a violation, was not justified, and Stanisic removed him for that reason, not because Dragan was involved in disarming or arrest of paramilitary formations which was the belief, I think, at the time; namely, since Mico Davidovic left, Dragan was kicked out. And this is the explanation that I believe I needed to offer to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to ask for this document to be marked for identification and we will inform the Chamber when we have the translation ready. It was -- it is a document that was brought here by the witness himself and we just need it to be translated into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, before we take any position on your request, I would like you to explain to us what significance you attach to the document. The document seems to show that Mr. Andan was finally moved out of his position because he had appropriated a gambling machine from the deposit, and so Mr. Stanisic's suspicion that this person, Mr. Andan, was, after all, not a reliable man may have been confirmed. But, in my view, nothing turns on this, in relation to the indictment, so I'm just wondering what is the relevance of this document, because I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Harhoff, the witness explained it in precisely the same way I would have explained it. The firing of Mr. Andan was previously explained by what the witness said. Namely, that he was involved in disarmament of paramilitary formations. But turns out he was not fired for that reason, which was the reason one could infer from what was stated in the statement of this witness but, instead, he was relieved of duty or fired for the purposes explained by this document. In other words, the witness confirmed that this is something that has shown that the earlier rumours were not correct, that he was relieved of duty in accordance with the rules of the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The document be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D348, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Davidovic, I'll show you now the next document, number --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe Tanja can help me, if this is P239. It's number 10 in the binder; tab 10 in the binder. 65 ter number 239. And P number -- I apologise, P number is 1269.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: These are the minutes of the extended session of the board of Serbian Republic, minister of the interior, held in the Kosuta facility on Mount Jahorina on 9 September.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please put up page 3 in the B/C/S on the screen. I'm interested in the last paragraph, which bears number 1. It's item number 1 on the last page. I don't know where it is in the English version. It's the sixth page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, I think you have had an opportunity to read this.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please move to the next page, item number 2 in the B/C/S version. It's the next item, next person. In the English version we should stay on the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Davidovic, you also know what was the position of Mr. Danilo Vukovic. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber who he was.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the function of Mr. Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we were making reports against Yellow Wasps and others, he was the one -- one of the operatives who was writing these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you just tell us what was the function of Mr. Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was the chief of the crime department in the CSB, Bijeljina. So he was chief of the crime department in CSB, Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, I have a short question for you. Disciplinary violations by both of these persons, Dragan Andan and Danilo Vukovic describe imposition of the most severe disciplinary measures; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that -- that the disciplinary procedure that was instigated at the time at this meeting that it was founded a well-founded and it had its base both in the rules and the laws. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, let us complete this topic, and I believe I will even complete the entire cross-examination today. You told us that almost all paramilitary formations entered Republika Srpska, claiming they were volunteers, patriots coming to fight on behalf of the Serbian People; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That's how they managed to fool some people, into believing that that was the real purpose. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Some of them took part in the patriotic struggle of the Serbian People and proven to actually be patriots.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just a small number of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The fact remains, actually what you just said now, that quite a few of them showed their true face very soon and that they started engaging in illegal activity, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That was the reason why, when Mico Stanisic visited you in Belgrade and when he said to you that he had observed precisely that and said that such individuals and groups should be fought against?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't in Belgrade. It was in Bijeljina. I don't know who else he talked to, but in Bijeljina he said that there were paramilitary formations that should be disarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me just briefly, I think you testified about that. Basically where was the main problem? You talked about local organs of authority, Crisis Staffs. Is that where the crux of the problem was with regard to the struggle against such units?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: You know what, you put questions and you offer a yes-or-no answer, as if this were a TV quiz show. I cannot give that kind of an answer. It is a complex question and it requires a serious broad answer. I cannot just say yes or no. If you allow me I will explain but that does require time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I do allow you to do that.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the beginning of the war, in Republika Srpska, there was a transformation of the system as whole. Crisis Staffs were established. Some kind of SAOs were established. And there was total lawlessness, in terms of the official organs of government that had functioned until then. Then there was a general call on the part of the high leadership - Karadzic, Krajisnik, Biljana Plavsic - calling volunteers to come to Republika Srpska to defend the Serb people from alleged threats to them, coming from the Muslims. A great deal of people responded to that. They came to Republika Srpska and they went to different municipalities. Some went to Herzegovina, Trebinje, Nevesinje, others went to Bijeljina, third groups went to Banja Luka, and so on. One of the first person who organised such arrivals was Arkan, Grey Wolfs, et cetera, different units who came to take part, allegedly, in the struggle, in terms of defending the Serb people. However, these were people who came with the sole intention of looting, killing, attaining some kind of material benefit. Then for the local authorities that had been organised in the meantime they did some things that were wrong, especially for normal people who lived at the time in Republika Srpska and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Members of other ethnic groups, like Croats and Muslims were being taken away, beaten up and killed even during the course of the night. Their property was looted and no one was held accountable for all of that. Throughout that time, the local authorities, the Crisis Staffs, the police, the reserve police and the active-duty police, made it possible for such paramilitary formations to operate, and they operated unhindered. When they carried out this kind of dirty work, when they created this feeling of fear and lawlessness, and when they were no longer in a position to loot those unfortunate Muslims because there was no property left, then they even started looking for Serbs who were well off and then they started taking away their property. It is it interesting that then they opposed -- then they imposed themselves on the local authorities. They started doing whatever they wanted to do. So then the problem was how to get rid of such persons. Then people started moaning, saying, Save us, help us, we cannot defend ourselves from these paramilitaries any longer. We don't have the force to oppose them. The Ministry of Interior, until then, had been linked with them, Bijeljina, Arkan is a classical example of that, that even happened in Zvornik where the Yellow Wasps were and then I was there as well. Then Brcko, the Berets and the Bozic brothers and all the rest, when they started killing and looting. And even when they started disobeying the local authorities then someone finally came to realise that they need to be expelled from there. When they turned into the very opposite, when they actually started harming them and when they did not share the booty as they did until then, then they wanted to get rid of them, Brcko, and to a large extent, Bijeljina was a case in point. It is only now that the question was put: How did it happen that these people managed to do that kind of thing when there were organs of government there? That is a consequence of such relations that existed. It's the local leadership that is responsible for that. However, I repeat once again this local leadership was not independent. It pursued the policy of the SDS, the political party that was in power in Republika Srpska. The SDS had a planned conceived policy of cleansing all areas where Muslims lived of those same Muslims. Whoever says that that is not the case, I claim with good arguments that they did that consciously, in an organised way, and it wasn't only the question of Bijeljina, Zvornik, Brcko, it was throughout Republika Srpska. The leadership of the SDS had planned, organised activities in terms of ethnically cleansing the Muslims. Whoever helped them -- well, that was the entire -- that was the core of the matter. That is what I have claim, that is what I have said at every point in time and I can say again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to explain to you -- I mean, you already explained that in the Krajisnik trial, so I didn't want you to repeat it, but now you explained, so thank you. I would just be interested in the following: As for Mr. Mico Stanisic, did you get absolute authority from him to fight against paramilitaries and all types of criminals, irrespective?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I did not have any reason not to have that kind of full powers given to me, and I must say that he did not hinder me in any way. He did not call me and ask what I was doing. He never called me and said, Release this person or that person. That is a fact and that is what I have to say.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could Mr. Cvijetic please keep his microphone off when the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When some local communities even claimed you to be an unwanted a person, a persona non grata, did you still receive the report of Mr. Stanisic and did he allow you to do everything that you were supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the case. I must say that he did not prevent me from carrying out the work I was doing in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Stanisic say to you that you should carry out a selection in terms of the types of crimes committed or the perpetrators of some kinds; for example, were you supposed to deal with some crimes others not or to arrest some perpetrates and others not?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. Please, I said at the very outset, when I talked to him, he gave me full powers without any limits. He said, Please arrest all paramilitaries wherever possible, wherever you can, irrespective of what was going on. You should act within the law, you should file criminal reports and so son. There was no dilemma involved whatsoever. I did not leave Bijeljina because I was expelled. I have to say that. Quite a few stories have been bandied about so I need to say something because I left during the course of the night. Because the federal minister, I was called in, I was ordered to return to Belgrade and to urgently go to Montenegro, and when I returned to Belgrade I was supposed to go back to Bijeljina yet again to continue doing what I had been doing. That had been the agreement, but everything changed. I went to Montenegro and after that I went to Kosovo, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, I think that you were talking about this special unit of the MUP of Republika Srpska and certain violations. Let us try to spell out the exact time involved. You are talking about the time when Mr. Stanisic was no longer minister of the interior; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute. I cannot speak exactly in terms of time now. I just know that Mico Stanisic insisted that the special unit from Sarajevo be included. I have to admit that I was against having them involved together with me in this action. However, since I knew that this unit was absolutely incapable of doing that that they had only 12 or 13 people who were professionally trained to carry that kind of thing out. However, Mico Stanisic insisted to involve them in the action to see how they would perform and that they should be one of the participants in this action. They did take part in this action. They carried this job out and that was it. I have to say another thing --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just one more question.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Wait a moment, let me finish what I was saying. Don't interrupt me. Later on I pointed that out in my statement, namely that this unit turned into its very opposite. In Zvornik, they did things that were even worse than what the Yellow Wasps had been doing. They turned into renegades, 150 men came and they were put up at the Drina Hotel and at Vidikovac after a while, now that is correct. I don't know how long Mico was minister. He did leave that job truth to tell, but I know that in 2003 or it was the end of the year, the citizens of Zvornik protested because of the problems they had with that special unit because out of the 150 men who had arrived, 100 of them were expelling Muslims they lived in their houses, their apartments, and in that way they practically continued doing what the Yellow Wasps had been doing. I cannot tell you which period this was, before or later. But it is a fact that this unit also turned into something that was contrary to what their original task had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You said and the transcript says that too. Towards the end of 2003. I assume that it's an obvious mistake, you meant -- tell me what year did you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I meant 1993. I really do apologise. Sorry, I got carried away.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, thank you for your testimony. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We don't have questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to make a request. I saw recently there was a request by the stenographer to ask the witness to slow down. I notice some parts of the transcript appear to have been having a difficult time following. I know that will be cleared up when someone has had a chance to listen to the tapes. What I'm asking is if can we recess early and I can start my cross-exam in the morning. We are way ahead of schedule in this witness now, and it will be easier, certainly for me, if I have the transcript, once it has had a chance to be checked and put in proper order. That will make me more efficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm also informed that our next witness can't start before Wednesday, at any rate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The Chamber was just considering this situation in which we, once again, find ourselves. And we're not exactly sure how to go about it. But, obviously, this is a result of an estimation of the length of the cross-examination that was obviously very far from -- from what the Defence actually took. And it's obvious that this makes it very difficult for the Chamber to plan the proceedings if -- if the estimations are so grossly erroneous. So I think the best way ahead is for the Chamber to remind the parties once again to be more accurate in their estimations of how much time they will need for examination-in-chief and for cross. Because the other way around, of course, when we get to the Defence cases ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would respectfully disagree that this is an result of our estimations. The estimations are only estimations. Because, Your Honours, we are bound to give our estimates way before the witness comes. Now, there are two aspects of it which definitely has a certain impact on the length of our cross-examination. It is it, first, the direct examination of the -- of the Office of the Prosecutor; and the second thing is the -- the interview of the witness that we conduct before -- if the witness, of course, accepts to be subject to interview of the Defence. Therefore, Your Honour, we gave the estimate maybe a couple of months ago, estimating that it is going to take far longer than -- than -- than it did. But we notified our friends from the Prosecutor. As soon as we were able to give a better estimate, we notified them that our cross-examination is going to be shortened. That is -- that is absolutely the best what we can do. I'm really sorry that we cannot be of more help, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis -- may I? I would -- I would like to add perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: There is a perhaps a third element, Mr. Hannis. That is the extent of the witness statement and the witness -- and the transcripts you are -- you are offering. And I noted that in this case there was no highlighting done. Is that for us to conclude that everything is --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That was our specific decision in this case to include it all because we thought it was necessary for you to see it all to evaluate his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would indicate, Your Honour, I guess I just wanted to remind the Defence about Rule 90(H) in the obligation to put to a witness in cross-examination their case, and there are some portions in this witness's statement where he talks directly about some things that Mr. Stanisic said to him or happened with them, and some of those didn't appear to be addressed, so I assume that is going to be addressed in the Defence case somehow, but it wasn't raised or challenged with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In this vein, Mr. Hannis, I alert you to the possibility, and I put it no higher than that, as you may be aware -- well, the background to what I'm about to say is the general concern about lost court time, and you would be aware that there is a division of views among individual Judges and, indeed, among Chambers as to whether the side whose case is being presented. At our stage, it's the Prosecution and at a later stage, it would be the other side, should have backup witnesses so that when these gaps occur, we are not sitting down counting the tiles on the ceiling. The -- we would have, in this Chamber, been invited to address the question some months ago when we deferred it indefinitely because as I said, it is something that is not yet settled throughout the Tribunal, and I appreciate the argument that the Prosecution has made in this vein about the inconvenience and impracticality of having witnesses sitting around in The Hague, who may then have to return and not go back but, of course, that has to be set off against the expense of simply running this Tribunal each day. It is a problem not peculiar to the -- to this Tribunal, not peculiar to this system, and it is certainly in my own country, I'm well aware of it, and heretofore I have been disinclined, bearing in mind the preference for the convenience of witnesses to have backup witnesses, but I alert you that circumstances may force me to go to the other side of that -- that argument. We may have to return to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am well familiar with that, Your Honour. In a previous case, I had a judge who at the beginning of the case, was penalising the Prosecution and subtracting time from their case allowed for -- or case in chief when we had some gaps because we finish -- later on, he withdrew that yellow card or red card and gave us the time back because he understood the difficulties and we have to engage victim witness in this discussion as well, because they are the ones that have the rule about five days, et cetera, but I just want to respond to what Mr. Zecevic said concerning the time estimates. I think if we went back through all the witnesses and counted up all the time estimates, I think you would find that there is more room for judgement on that side. I understand here, I think the original estimate was six hours. Now that original estimate of six hours had be based in part on the fact that this was a 92 ter witness and we were going to put in transcripts from five days of testimony and a written statement that was 50-some pages. And I don't know what the witness said during his one-on-one interview with Mr. Cvijetic on Sunday that made him change his mind and go from six hours to what turned out to be one and a half, but it didn't appear to be that he went through and said, Everything I said in my statement is not true, I withdraw it. So I think it could have been a better estimate, and we could have known sooner than -- than yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Anyway we accept we're in the realm of art not science. One other matter, Mr. Hannis. Looking at the week's schedule, we -- we were scheduled to deal with this matter of exhumations on Friday. We were wondering, whether you, and I say you plural, would be prepared, inasmuch as we will have some time tomorrow to deal with it then. I'm merely throwing that out now. I don't expect either side to be in a position to respond definitively but think about it overnight and it may very well be that it is something that the time could usefully be used for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: There is perhaps something else to take into account, that is the testimony of ST-210, which I don't think will take the two days scheduled now. So if we can perhaps re-plan the arguments on exhumations and perhaps advance a little bit ST-210, we can win a day, day and a half, for perhaps another witness, if it can be organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will discuss that with the assigned attorney and with my learned friends across the way, and we'll see what we can do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So we take the adjournment until 9.00, tomorrow in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 24th day of August, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
